items.title: Statistical experiments
items.statement: An experiment is a measurable sample space (X,A) together with a set Θ of parameter labels and a family (P_θ)_{θ∈Θ} of probability measures on (X,A). The family consists of sampling laws; it does not assert that Θ is measurable, that θ↦P_θ is measurable, or that all laws are realized on one specified probability space. If data are realized as a random element, its law is the pushforward law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]].

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §§1.3.6 and 1.4.1, PDF pp. 20–23
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, §6, PDF pp. 6–7

items.title: Parametric statistical models
items.statement: For an experiment on (X,A), write P(X,A) for its set of probability measures. A parametric statistical model is the parameter map P:Θ→P(X,A), θ↦P_θ, regarded together with its parameter set Θ and sample space. The map need not be injective. Unless a measurable structure on Θ is supplied separately, no measurability of this map is asserted.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §§1.3.6 and 1.4.1, PDF pp. 20–23
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, §6, PDF pp. 6–7

items.title: Parameter-measurable statistical models as kernels
items.statement: If (Θ,T) is a measurable parameter space, a Markov (probability) kernel representation of an experiment on (X,A) is a function K:Θ×A→[0,1] such that K(θ,·) is a probability measure on (X,A) for every θ and, for every A∈A and every Borel set C⊆[0,1] (the sigma-algebra generated by relatively open subsets U∩[0,1] with U open in R), {θ∈Θ:K(θ,A)∈C}∈T. It represents the given model exactly when K(θ,A)=P_θ(A) for every θ and A. This is an additional parameter-measurability condition, not part of an arbitrary experiment.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §§1.3.6, 1.4.1 and 5.1, PDF pp. 20–23 and 100–102
Botond Szabó and Aad van der Vaart, Bayesian Statistics, lecture notes, §1.1, Definition 1.1 and the statistical-model kernel conditions following it

items.title: Observational equivalence
items.statement: In a parametric model P:Θ→P(X,A), parameters θ and η are observationally equivalent, written θ∼η, exactly when P_θ=P_η as measures; equivalently, P_θ(A)=P_η(A) for every A∈A. Thus equivalent parameter values give the same sampling law, even when θ≠η.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §§1.3.6 and 1.4.1, PDF pp. 20–23
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, §6, PDF pp. 6–7

items.title: Estimands on a statistical model
items.statement: For a parametric model with parameter set Θ, an estimand (parameter target) is a specified function ψ:Θ→T₀ into a target set T₀. No measurable structure on Θ or T₀ is assumed by this definition.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §1.4.1, PDF pp. 22–23
Peter Hoff, Statistical Decision Problems, pp. 1–2

items.title: Identifiability of an estimand
items.statement: An estimand ψ:Θ→T₀ is identifiable in the model P if ψ(θ)=ψ(η) whenever θ∼η (equivalently, whenever P_θ=P_η). The model itself is identifiable when its identity estimand id_Θ is identifiable, which is equivalent to injectivity of θ↦P_θ.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §§1.3.5–1.3.6, PDF pp. 19–21
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, §6, PDF pp. 6–7

items.title: Identifiability is constancy on observational classes
items.statement: Let P:Θ→P(X,A) be a parametric model, ψ:Θ→T₀ an estimand, and M=P(Θ) the set of model laws. The following are equivalent: (i) ψ is identifiable; (ii) ψ is constant on every observational equivalence class [θ]={η∈Θ:η∼θ}; (iii) there is a unique function ψ̄:M→T₀ such that ψ=ψ̄∘P. No measurable structure or measurable factorization is asserted.
items.strategy: Direct. First note that equality of probability measures makes observational equivalence an equivalence relation. Its class-constancy condition is exactly the definition of estimand identifiability. A factor through M implies that equal laws have equal target values. Conversely, under identifiability define ψ̄(P_θ)=ψ(θ); show this is independent of the representative, then use that every point of M has a representative to prove existence and uniqueness. This constructs the map from its graph and uses no choice axiom.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §§1.3.5–1.3.6, PDF pp. 19–21
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, §6, PDF pp. 6–7

title: Statistical Experiments, Models and Identifiability — Examples

items.title: Identifiable Bernoulli model and parameter target
items.statement: On X={0,1} with all subsets measurable and parameter set Θ=[0,1], define P_p({1})=p and P_p({0})=1−p. This is an identifiable statistical model, and the target ψ(p)=p is identifiable.
items.strategy: Direct finite verification. For each p, define P_p(A)=p·1_{1∈A}+(1−p)·1_{0∈A}; check nonnegative singleton masses, total mass one and additivity on the finite sample space. Equality of laws forces equality of their mass on {1}, hence equality of parameters and targets.

items.title: A redundant Bernoulli parameterization has a nonidentifiable coordinate
items.statement: Let Θ={(u,v)∈[0,1]^2:u+v≤1}, X={0,1}, and P_{u,v}({1})=u+v, P_{u,v}({0})=1−u−v. The first-coordinate target ψ(u,v)=u is not identifiable.
items.strategy: Direct finite verification. Check that every admissible pair gives a probability law. The distinct parameters (1/5,1/2) and (3/10,2/5) have the same sum 7/10, so they give equal laws but different first-coordinate targets.
